new_entities.name: Clomiphene for anovulatory infertility
new_entities.description: Use of clomiphene citrate as an ovulation-induction treatment for women with anovulatory infertility, particularly PCOS.

new_entities.name: Live birth rate
new_entities.description: The probability of delivering a live infant after fertility treatment or conception.

edges.effect_quant: Clomiphene remains an active fertility drug, but the live-birth evidence is older and weaker than for letrozole. The 2016 Cochrane update concluded clomiphene is superior to placebo for pregnancy outcomes and remains an accepted first-line oral inducer, while newer comparative meta-analysis shows it is consistently outperformed by letrozole for live birth.
edges.population: women with anovulatory infertility, especially women with PCOS undergoing first-line ovulation induction
edges.mechanism: Clomiphene blocks estrogen receptors centrally, increasing gonadotropin release and triggering follicular recruitment and ovulation. Its main limitation is that the same anti-estrogenic action can also impair endometrial receptivity or cervical mucus, which likely explains why it helps but does not lead the field anymore.
edges.summary: Clomiphene is still a genuinely active ovulation-induction drug, not a placebo-like relic. The more careful modern interpretation is that it can improve fertility and live-birth outcomes in anovulatory women, but it now sits as a useful older standard rather than the best-performing first-line option.
edges.caveats: Live-birth reporting is sparse in the older clomiphene literature, and many trials focus on pregnancy or ovulation rather than delivery. This edge should therefore be read as modestly favorable, with the explicit understanding that letrozole generally performs better.
